newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Samsung says seeking partner in Fokker rescue.
newsitem.headline: Samsung says seeking partner in Fokker rescue.

text.p: South Korea's Samsung Aerospace Industries said on Wednesday it had invited other domestic companies to join it in a rescue of Dutch planemaker Fokker NV.
But Samsung denied this was slowing down the deal and said the Seoul government was not involved in any aspect of its bid for the stricken company.
Dutch media reports have suggested a review of the rescue deal by the Seoul government might be holding things up.

"We approached several local companies when we started negotiations with the Dutch government and asked whether they were interested in participating in the Fokker takeover," said Shin Sang-yong, a spokesman for Samsung Aerospace.
"We can't say what the response was. But we can tell you that neither the Korean government nor the possible involvement of other companies are at issue here."
Samsung Group spokesman Kim Jin-soo said Hyundai Group and Daewoo Group were offered a chance to participate in the buyout in July and August.
"We have informally asked Hyundai and Daewoo whether they were interested due to the vastness of the investment," said Kim. "I believe they haven't made up their minds yet."
Kim denied the South Korean government would have any say in the project.
"The only government approval Samsung needs is from the central Bank of Korea on capital investment abroad," he said.

Yu Jeong-yeol, deputy director of the aerospace industry division at the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said: "It's a private project paid for by a private company. The government can't tell Samsung what to do."

"We would, however, like to see more companies participating in the takeover due to the dangers of a huge investment overseas by a single company. But that is only our wish. How Samsung wants to take over Fokker is its own business."
The Samsung spokesmen said it was unclear when the Fokker deal would be concluded.
"The deal has been imminent for the last month or so. It's hard to say when it is expected to be agreed upon," Shin said.
The Dutch government has expressed mounting worries that eight months after the planemaker was declared bankrupt, there is still no agreement on a plan to relaunch Fokker.

Samsung, seen as an Asian savior for Fokker, was given an exclusive look into Fokker's books in September by court-appointed administrators, with a view to a possible takeover of Fokker's core plane-making business.
The Samsung Group, Samsung Aerospace's parent, has deep pockets and great ambitions in aerospace.

Fokker, founded in 1919 by Dutch aviation pioneer Anthony Fokker, is one of the oldest names in the industry and its F27 Friendship turboprop, launched in 1957, was one of the industry's biggest commercial successes.

Samsung views Fokker as a way of breaking into the global aerospace industry, but industry analysts say the company does not want to assume all the risks and has sought major investment by the Dutch state.
The Dutch government has indicated support but Samsung is said to have balked at demands for long-term job guarantees in the Netherlands.
The Samsung spokesmen declined to comment on the contents of discussions with Fokker and the Dutch government.
South Korean media reports have said Samsung was ready to sink $180 million into acquiring a 70 percent stake in Fokker.
